title: Five dates for one number: observation, publication, availability, ingestion — and the time zone

explain.prompt: The trader asks: “The stocks for the week ending 17 June 2022 are in our database — when could we actually have traded on that number?” In 4–6 sentences with your numbers: explain the dates attached to each weekly figure, the publication lags you found, why ingested_at cannot be used as the availability time for 2019, and why the UTC hour of the release changes during the year.
rubric: Each figure has an observation date (the week ending Friday), a publication time (release date at 10:30 New York), an availability time (the same instant in UTC — when the desk could act), an ingestion time (when our database stored it) and, for revised data, a vintage.

Usual lag: 5 days (Friday → Wednesday) for 278 of 314 reports; 6 days for 35 (a Monday holiday, or a holiday on the Wednesday, pushes it to Thursday); 12 days once — the week ending 17 Jun 2022 was published on 29 Jun 2022, so it was not tradable for 12 days.

61 records were ingested on 2 Mar 2020 when the database was created (backfill): their ingested_at says nothing about when the market knew them; for those, availability must come from the release calendar.
10:30 New York is 15:30 UTC in winter and 14:30 UTC in summer (110 vs 204 releases): converting with the time zone, not a fixed offset, keeps the availability exact across US DST changes.
The surprise (actual change − consensus) is the new information of a release; the level of stocks is mostly known in advance — this is what moves prices at 10:30 and what 3.2–3.5 use.
